analysis.one_liner: Banned civilian handgun possession and sales, with exceptions for police, the military, security guards, and licensed shooting clubs.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Judiciary Committee's crime subcommittee — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and died when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it a federal crime to make, sell, buy, or personally own a handgun or handgun ammunition. It carved out exceptions for the armed forces, police, registered private security companies, and licensed target-shooting clubs whose guns stay locked up at the club. People who turned in a handgun within 180 days would be paid at least $25 or its market value; after that, someone caught with one faced up to five years in prison and a $5,000 fine.
analysis.who_benefits: People living with high rates of handgun violence — the bill's own findings cite record handgun homicides, guns in schools, and at least $4 billion a year in shooting-related medical costs [S3]. Police and the military keep their weapons, and private security firms and target clubs keep operating under registration and licensing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities hit hardest by handgun violence

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits all civilian manufacture, sale, purchase, and possession of handguns and handgun ammunition, with narrow exceptions for the military, law enforcement, registered security guard services, and licensed handgun clubs [S2][S3].

Pays people who voluntarily surrender a handgun within 180 days of enactment at least $25 or its fair market value, and shields late surrenderers from criminal prosecution in exchange for a civil penalty of up to $500 [S2][S3].
Requires licensed clubs and registered security services to store guns securely, keep records, and report lost or stolen handguns, with seizure and forfeiture of guns used in violations [S2][S3].
The bill's findings cite handgun homicides setting records every year since 1987, easy access to guns in schools, and $4 billion a year in emergency and hospital care from gun injuries [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Handgun owners — whom the bill itself counts at more than 70 million — would have to surrender or lose their guns or face up to five years in prison and a $5,000 fine [S3]. Handgun manufacturers, importers, and dealers lose nearly their entire civilian market, allowed only to supply the exempted police, military, security, and club channels with Treasury approval [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Current handgun owners and the gun industry

drawbacks.text: Roughly 70 million handguns were already privately held when the bill was introduced, by the bill's own count, and the ban would have criminalized the possession of ordinary people who had done nothing wrong, on penalty of five years in prison [S3].

The exceptions system relies on the Treasury Secretary approving manufacturers and dealers to supply police, military, security firms, and clubs — a large licensing and enforcement undertaking with mandatory recordkeeping and inspection, and civil penalties up to $1,000 and criminal penalties up to five years for record and reporting failures [S2][S3].

Home defense is a common reason for ownership; the bill's own findings argue handguns in the home are more likely to endanger residents than to protect them, but many gun owners reject that premise and would bear the loss of their property with it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case for reducing handgun deaths was serious, and the bill's buy-back and club-licensing design was a genuine attempt to ease the transition. But the burden of a near-total ban would fall heavily on tens of millions of ordinary owners, and the exemption machinery — clubs, security firms, and a licensed dealer channel approved by the Treasury Secretary — would still keep handguns flowing to a wide set of non-police users. Whether the safety gains would justify criminalizing possession at that scale was never tested, because the bill never received a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 1993, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then sent to its crime subcommittee a few days later — and nothing ever happened after that; no hearing, no markup, no floor vote before the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Major Owens (D-NY) introduced the Public Health and Safety Act of 1993 on September 23, 1993, with introductory remarks in the Congressional Record [S1][S5].

The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on September 23, 1993, and to the Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice on September 27, 1993 — the last action of any kind recorded for the bill [S5].
Fourteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill, all from the same party as the sponsor; no Republican signed on [S4].
The bill died in subcommittee when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, without ever receiving a committee vote or a floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Current handgun owners kept their guns and their rights, and the handgun industry kept its civilian market — the ban was never enacted, so the status quo won by default.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun owners and the handgun industry

for.name: Rep. Major Owens
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it with remarks on the House floor [S1][S5].

for.name: 14 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Reps. Reynolds, Clay, Nadler, Norton, Lewis of Georgia, Velazquez, Dellums, Meek, and Hastings

against.name: House Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice
against.role: Subcommittee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 27, 1993 and never acted on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote; the bill sat until the Congress ended [S5].

against.name: National Rifle Association and allied gun-rights groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed handgun prohibition measures of this era as a matter of well-documented public advocacy; the congressional record contains no direct action by them on this specific bill.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 14 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support, and the bill died in committee in a Democratic-controlled House without ever coming to a vote [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Handgun and ammunition manufacturers, importers, and dealers
industries.note: The bill would have eliminated their civilian market entirely; licensed dealers could operate only to supply exempted police, military, security, and club customers with Treasury approval [S2][S3]. The industry's interest in continued civilian sales ran against the bill's public-safety aim.

Clubs would become the only legal civilian channel for handgun use, requiring secure on-site or police storage, member background checks, recordkeeping, and a $25 annual fee [S3]. Their members keep the sport but lose individual possession.
Registered security firms would keep their handguns under lockup, recordkeeping, and reporting rules, paying a $50 annual registration fee [S3].
